paragraphs: Mental rotation lets people compare objects even when they see them from different viewpoints. This paper develops a computational account of that ability, asking whether a model that builds spatial representations and actively simulates rotations can reproduce human performance. Its design draws on previous behavioral research and additional virtual-reality experiments in which participants could sometimes manipulate the objects they were comparing.

The model connects three components. An equivariant neural encoder converts images into three-dimensional spatial representations. A second encoder turns those representations into symbolic object descriptions. A neural decision agent compares the descriptions and uses a recurrent connection to prescribe further rotation simulations within the model’s internal three-dimensional space.

The authors report that the model captures participants’ accuracy, response times, and behavior in both their experiments and earlier studies. Removing components in ablation studies demonstrates that each is necessary for the model’s reported performance. These findings support combining neural perception, spatial structure, and symbolic descriptions as a useful approach to modeling human spatial reasoning.
icml-2026-a-deep-learning-model-of-menta.tldr: A model combining spatial encoding, symbolic descriptions, and simulated rotations reproduces several aspects of human mental-rotation behavior.

paragraphs: An LLM’s internal activations contain information that can be difficult to express or inspect directly. This paper studies models trained to receive those activations and answer natural-language questions about them. The authors call these models Activation Oracles and investigate whether their explanatory abilities extend well beyond the narrow settings used to train them.

The study evaluates generalization to substantially different settings and examines the effect of diversifying training data. Activation Oracles recover information introduced through another model’s fine-tuning, including biographical knowledge and malign propensities, even when that information is absent from the input text. They do this despite never having trained on activations from a fine-tuned model.

Across four downstream tasks, even narrowly trained models generalize well, while additional classification and self-supervised context-prediction data consistently improve performance. The strongest oracles match or beat white-box baselines on all four tasks and the strongest overall baseline on three. The results suggest that varied question-answering training can develop a broader ability to verbalize information contained in activations.
icml-2026-activation-oracles-training-an.tldr: Activation Oracles answer questions about LLM activations and show strong generalization, with more diverse training improving their explanations.

paragraphs: Deep graph neural networks can repeatedly mix neighboring information until different nodes have nearly indistinguishable representations. Familiar explanations of this oversmoothing rely on sufficiently bounded network weights. Larger weights may compensate for smoothing, so the architecture could theoretically learn to avoid it. This paper asks why training often fails to find that solution.

The authors examine backward oversmoothing: the errors used to train the network can themselves become smoothed as they travel from outputs toward inputs. With nonlinear transformations, they emphasize the interaction between this backward process and the smoothing of representations during the forward pass. The difficulty therefore concerns how learning signals propagate, as well as what the network can represent.

Their analysis proves the existence of many spurious stationary points associated with backward oversmoothing, where training the final layer leaves the entire network stationary. They also identify regions with almost no gradient despite high loss. The authors show that this phenomenon is specific to graph networks in their analysis and need not occur in multilayer perceptrons.
icml-2026-backward-oversmoothing-why-is-.tldr: Backward oversmoothing helps explain why deep graph networks can stop learning while their prediction loss remains high.

paragraphs: State space models offer efficient sequence processing, but applying them to images introduces structural difficulties. Existing vision versions often flatten image patches using manually chosen scanning patterns. These patterns impose a fixed geometry on processing. Their sequential, self-referential design also makes it difficult to support queries between separate information streams, which matters for tasks such as combining multiple views into a three-dimensional representation.

Deformba addresses both issues through context-adaptive spatial processing and state fusion. It dynamically augments spatial structural information while retaining the linear complexity associated with state space models. It also supports multimodal fusion analogous to cross attention, providing a way for distinct streams of information to interact.

The authors evaluate the approach on image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, semantic segmentation, and three-dimensional bird’s-eye-view perception. They report strong performance across these visual benchmarks. The contribution is a more adaptable way to use state space models for perception, extending their spatial processing and fusion capabilities while preserving their favorable computational scaling.
icml-2026-deformba-vision-state-space-mo.tldr: Deformba adds adaptive spatial processing and cross-stream fusion to vision state space models while retaining linear complexity.

paragraphs: A model can perform well by exploiting correlations in its training data that do not reflect the signals relevant to its task. This paper connects that problem to a causal account of dataset bias. Its Standard Anti-Causal Model organizes bias mechanisms into a shared framework and derives a conditional independence criterion for causal stability.

To make that criterion useful during training, the authors introduce two estimators of conditional distance correlation, DISCO_m and sDISCO. These provide an efficient, scalable way to measure the relevant dependence and incorporate independence regularization into models trained with gradients. The approach connects a theoretical description of unwanted relationships to a quantity that a learning algorithm can act on.

Across six datasets, the methods consistently outperform or remain competitive with existing approaches to mitigating observed biases. They also require fewer hyperparameters and extend to settings involving multiple biases. The stated findings support the practical value of the causal framework: its independence criterion leads to usable training tools with competitive empirical results across the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-disco-mitigating-bias-in-deep-.tldr: DISCO turns a causal independence criterion into scalable training regularizers that mitigate observed dataset biases.

paragraphs: Transformer attention usually computes separate query, key, and value projections. This paper tests how much that separation contributes by studying shared keys and values, shared queries and keys, and a single shared projection. Because sharing queries and keys produces symmetric attention maps, the authors also investigate two-dimensional positional encodings as a way to introduce asymmetry.

Experiments cover synthetic tasks, vision, and language modeling. Across these settings, the variants perform comparably to standard attention and sometimes better. In language modeling, sharing keys and values cuts the key-value cache by 50% with a reported 3.1% perplexity degradation. The authors attribute its quality preservation to keys and values being able to share a representational space, whereas sharing queries and keys disrupts directionality.

Projection sharing also combines with attention-head sharing. Shared keys and values with GQA-4 reduce the cache by 87.5%, and combining them with MQA reduces it by 96.9%. These results identify another way to reduce transformer memory demands, with particular relevance to inference on devices with limited memory.
icml-2026-do-transformers-need-three-pro.tldr: Sharing attention projections can preserve much of transformer quality while substantially reducing key-value cache memory.

paragraphs: A benchmark score describes performance on a particular collection of questions, but evaluators often want to infer performance on other similar questions. This paper formally separates these goals: benchmark accuracy concerns the observed test items, while generalized accuracy concerns the wider population of potential items. Confusing them can introduce hidden assumptions or produce invalid uncertainty estimates.

The authors use generalized linear mixed models to analyze evaluation results. They study the approach in simulations and in evaluations of 22 API-accessible frontier language models on three benchmarks. In these settings, the statistical analysis produces correct estimates of generalized accuracy and quantifies uncertainty more efficiently than existing approaches that do not use regression.

The model also provides context beyond an overall score. Variance decomposition helps describe sources of variation in evaluation results, while item-difficulty estimates reveal differences among benchmark questions. These outputs make the analysis useful for understanding both model performance and benchmark construction, alongside the central task of estimating how performance may extend to similar test items.
icml-2026-expanding-the-ai-evaluation-to.tldr: Statistical mixed models help distinguish benchmark scores from broader accuracy and provide more informative uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: LLMs can help discover programs that solve optimization problems, but evaluating every candidate against a fixed distribution of instances can encourage overfitting. A heuristic may become effective on familiar instances while generalizing poorly when the distribution changes. Algorithm Space Response Oracles, or ASRO, addresses this by making the training challenges evolve alongside the solver.

The framework represents solver programs and instance-generator programs as opposing players in a two-player zero-sum game. It maintains growing collections of strategies for both sides. LLM-based response oracles propose new programs against mixtures of the opponent’s existing strategies, allowing the interaction to create an adaptive curriculum instead of relying on a static evaluation set.

Across multiple combinatorial optimization domains, ASRO consistently outperforms static-training heuristic-discovery baselines that use the same underlying program-search mechanisms. The authors report substantially better generalization and robustness on diverse and out-of-distribution instances. This comparison supports the value of changing how candidate programs encounter challenges, while keeping the underlying search machinery comparable.
icml-2026-game-theoretic-co-evolution-fo.tldr: ASRO co-evolves solver and instance-generator programs to improve the generalization of LLM-discovered optimization heuristics.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can be overly confident on inputs outside their training distribution. Geometrically Constrained Outlier Synthesis addresses this during training by constructing artificial outliers in the model’s hidden feature space. Its central idea is to use the geometry of familiar data when deciding where those outliers should lie, so they provide useful examples near the boundary of the learned distribution.

The synthesis has two stages. A subspace capturing dominant feature variation helps identify directions away from the learned data manifold. A shell based on calibration-set quantiles then controls how far synthesized points move. The shell keeps samples from becoming either too easy to recognize or too similar to familiar data. A contrastive objective encourages separation between familiar and unfamiliar samples in a selected score space.

Using energy-based inference, GCOS outperforms state-of-the-art methods on evaluated near-OOD benchmarks, where outliers share the familiar data’s semantic domain. The authors also explore conformal inference, translating uncertainty scores into statistically valid p-values and enabling error-controlled thresholds. That extension is presented as a pathway toward more predictable detection.
icml-2026-geometrically-constrained-outl.tldr: GCOS uses feature-space geometry to synthesize useful training outliers and improves detection of unfamiliar inputs from related semantic domains.

paragraphs: Learning a graph’s structure means deciding which nodes should be connected so that the graph captures useful relationships. That becomes expensive for large graphs, especially when new nodes arrive and existing methods require the structure to be learned again. GraphFLEx targets both the initial search cost and the cost of maintaining a graph as it expands.

The framework combines clustering and coarsening to identify structurally relevant subsets of nodes. It restricts possible edge formation to those subsets, sharply reducing the search space and enabling incremental updates. This makes the selection of candidate connections a central part of scaling graph structure learning, rather than treating every potential connection as equally relevant.

GraphFLEx offers 48 configurations through different combinations of learning paradigms, coarsening strategies, and clustering methods. Evaluations across 26 datasets and graph neural network architectures report state-of-the-art performance with significantly improved scalability. The framework therefore provides several ways to adapt the same search-reduction principle to different graph settings and learning objectives.
icml-2026-graphflex-unsupervised-structu.tldr: GraphFLEx makes graph structure learning more scalable by restricting candidate edges and supporting incremental updates as graphs grow.

paragraphs: Vision-language systems need resources that reflect people with limb differences if they are to interpret those contexts effectively. This paper introduces IVQA-LD, a dataset and evaluation benchmark focused on limb-aware visual understanding, together with a strategy for adapting models. The work treats body structure and limb-specific meaning as central parts of the learning problem.

The dataset covers all eight limb-deficiency types across varied real-world scenarios. Its organization includes 96 limb-affected action categories and 68 functional classes drawn from internationally recognized classification frameworks. Expert annotations support 80,000 visual question-answer pairs across eight tasks, including locating visual content, quantitative reasoning, functional classification, and generating instructions.

Benchmarking leading vision-language models reveals difficulties across every task. The authors then introduce Body-centric Structure-aware Initialization, which aligns model representations with limb-specific semantics. Models fine-tuned on IVQA-LD using this strategy show significant improvements across all tasks. The contribution combines a structured resource for identifying shortcomings with a model-adaptation approach that improves performance on the resulting benchmark.
icml-2026-ivqa-ld-inclusive-multimodal-u.tldr: IVQA-LD exposes gaps in limb-aware vision-language understanding and provides a dataset and adaptation strategy that improve evaluated performance.

paragraphs: In many scientific applications, valid samples must satisfy exact equalities. Such constraints place the data on a restricted geometric set within the surrounding space. The paper addresses mathematical difficulties that arise when generative models attempt to learn distributions with this structure, focusing on a modification of the training distribution that remains aware of the constraints.

The proposed method perturbs the data so that the modified distribution occupies the full dimension of the ambient space. The perturbation still implicitly incorporates the geometry of the original constraint manifold. This combination is the central design choice: the distribution gains the dimensional support needed to address known modeling pitfalls while retaining information about the structure that makes samples valid.

The authors describe the modification as computationally inexpensive, mathematically justified, and flexible. Through theoretical analysis and experiments on several representative tasks, they show consistent recovery of the data distribution and stable sampling with both diffusion models and normalizing flows. The findings support constraint-aware distribution modification as a useful approach across these two generative-model families.
icml-2026-manifold-aware-perturbations-f.tldr: Constraint-aware perturbations help diffusion models and normalizing flows learn equality-constrained distributions and sample stably.

paragraphs: Coordinating multiple agents can improve reasoning, but the benefit depends on how the system is organized and what the task requires. This paper addresses both system design and evaluation. It argues that sequential, code-level orchestration makes global reasoning about a system difficult, while existing deployments often lack clear evidence of an advantage over a single agent.

MAS-Orchestra trains orchestration through function-calling reinforcement learning and generates an entire multi-agent system at once. Complex subagents are represented as callable functions, hiding their internal execution details so the orchestrator can reason about the overall structure. The accompanying MASBENCH evaluates tasks along five dimensions: Depth, Horizon, Breadth, Parallel, and Robustness.

The analysis finds that gains depend critically on task structure, verification protocols, and the abilities of both orchestrator and subagents. Guided by those findings, MAS-Orchestra consistently improves results on public mathematical-reasoning, multi-hop question-answering, and search-based question-answering benchmarks, with more than tenfold efficiency over strong baselines. The work makes the conditional nature of multi-agent benefits central to their design and assessment.
icml-2026-mas-orchestra-understanding-an.tldr: MAS-Orchestra trains whole-system agent coordination, while MASBENCH shows that multi-agent gains depend on task structure and agent capabilities.

paragraphs: A correct model output does not establish that the model used its normal internal mechanisms to produce it. This paper studies how to detect anomalous mechanisms by asking whether a small trusted set of samples can explain a test output. A failure of this functional attribution serves as a signal that the model may be behaving abnormally.

The method uses influence functions and sampling in parameter space to measure functional coupling between test samples and trusted reference samples. This reframes detection around relationships in model behavior. It addresses concerns with existing latent-space methods, which can be vulnerable to obfuscation, and methods tied to specific architectures or modalities.

For vision backdoors, the method achieves an average Defense Effectiveness Rating of 0.93 on BackdoorBench across seven attacks and four datasets, compared with 0.83 for the next-best method. It also improves detection of several LLM backdoor types, including explicitly obfuscated models. Evidence for detecting adversarial and out-of-distribution samples is preliminary, as is the broader finding that it can distinguish multiple anomalous mechanisms within one model.
icml-2026-mechanistic-anomaly-detection-.tldr: Functional attribution detects anomalous model behavior by testing whether trusted examples can explain a model’s output.

paragraphs: This paper studies anonymous multi-agent path finding, where robots must reach a set of targets on a finite, connected graph. It expresses the task as a multi-marginal optimal transport problem. Although that formulation is generally exponentially large, the authors identify an underlying Markovian structure that reduces it to a linear program of polynomial size.

For the anonymous setting, they establish conditions under which the linear program is feasible and totally unimodular. Under those conditions, it produces minimum-cost, integral transports with no overlap in space and time. Integrality matters because the resulting assignments describe discrete movements instead of dividing a robot fractionally among alternative routes.

To handle larger problems, the authors introduce a probabilistic Schrödinger bridge formulation. Under standard assumptions, this becomes an entropy-regularized transport problem solvable by Sinkhorn-type iteration. Its fractional solution guides a smaller linear program, which yields near-optimal integral transports with substantially reduced complexity. Experiments demonstrate the optimality and scalability of the approaches, distinguishing the exact formulation from the scalable near-optimal route.
icml-2026-optimal-and-scalable-mapf-via-.tldr: A transport formulation yields optimal anonymous robot paths under stated conditions, while a probabilistic approximation enables scalable near-optimal solutions.

paragraphs: Certified training aims to make neural networks both accurate and provably robust to adversarial perturbations. These goals can conflict: a configuration that improves certified accuracy may reduce accuracy on ordinary inputs. This paper argues that comparing methods through one chosen configuration can therefore misrepresent their overall performance and obscure the trade-offs available to users.

The authors compare Pareto fronts, which collect configurations where improving one accuracy measure requires sacrificing the other. They use automated multi-objective hyperparameter optimization to find these configurations for each method. This creates a method-agnostic comparison across the natural-versus-certified accuracy trade-off, rather than relying on a single operating point selected separately for each approach.

The search often reveals that previously reported configurations were substantially undertuned. Better tuning produces superior results and a new state of the art. Comparing the resulting fronts also makes earlier advances appear less pronounced and reveals previously unreported complementarities between methods. The findings show that conclusions about progress can change when evaluation accounts for both tuning and the full trade-off.
icml-2026-rethinking-evaluation-paradigm.tldr: Comparing full accuracy–robustness trade-offs reveals undertuned certified-training methods and changes conclusions about their relative performance.

paragraphs: Determining whether a text appeared in an LLM’s pretraining data matters for investigating privacy leakage and data contamination. Existing detection methods often summarize isolated token probabilities, such as focusing on particularly unlikely tokens. This paper instead examines how probabilities change across a sequence, treating their evolution as potentially informative evidence about memorization.

Adaptive Entropic Convolutional Analysis, or AECA, represents the sequence of token probabilities as a dynamic signal. It combines calibration with convolutional filtering to capture patterns in that signal. The motivating intuition is that memorized sequences have different volatility patterns from sequences handled through inference, making relationships across tokens useful for detection.

On the WikiMIA benchmark, the authors report improvements of up to 1.5% in average AUC over previous methods. The advantage is especially pronounced for longer texts. These findings support considering sequence-wide probability dynamics alongside the local statistics that have dominated earlier detection approaches. The reported result concerns improved discrimination on the benchmark, with the strongest gains appearing in its long-text scenarios.
icml-2026-rethinking-pretraining-data-de.tldr: AECA detects possible pretraining membership from sequence-wide probability dynamics, improving WikiMIA results especially for long texts.

paragraphs: Designing rewards by hand can make reinforcement learning difficult to apply. Human feedback offers another route, and discrete ratings can provide richer supervision than choosing between two trajectories. This paper develops Ranked Return Regression for RL, or R4, to learn rewards from trajectory–rating pairs such as sequences of behavior labeled bad, neutral, or good.

R4 uses a ranking mean squared error loss that treats ratings as ordinal targets. The ordering of the categories is therefore central to what the method learns. The authors also provide a formal characterization of the method’s solution set: under mild assumptions, it is both minimal and complete. These guarantees distinguish the approach from prior rating-based methods described in the paper.

The empirical evaluation uses both human-provided and simulated ratings on robotic benchmarks from OpenAI Gym and the DeepMind Control Suite. R4 consistently matches or outperforms existing rating-based and preference-based reinforcement-learning methods. The results support ordinal ratings as a practical source of reward supervision, paired with an objective that has stated theoretical guarantees.
icml-2026-reward-learning-through-rankin.tldr: R4 learns rewards from ordered human ratings using a ranking loss with formal guarantees and competitive robotic-benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Subjective language-model evaluation often asks people to choose the better of two responses, then combines those choices into a ranking. The paper argues that the commonly used Bradley–Terry framework forces varied preferences into a single total order and violates basic social-choice principles. It studies an alternative that allows pairwise preferences to retain more of their structure.

Maximal lotteries aggregate pairwise preferences without assumptions about that structure. However, the authors show that these lotteries can still be highly sensitive to differences among annotators and prompts. They introduce robust lotteries to address this problem by optimizing worst-case performance under plausible changes in the preference data.

On large-scale preference datasets, robust lotteries provide more reliable win-rate guarantees across the annotator distribution and identify a stable set of top-performing models. The result matters because a leaderboard’s conclusions can depend on whose judgments and which prompts are represented. The method explicitly accounts for plausible shifts in that evidence when determining which models remain strong choices.
icml-2026-robust-ai-evaluation-through-m.tldr: Robust lotteries aggregate subjective model comparisons while protecting against plausible shifts in annotator and prompt preferences.

paragraphs: Debiased machine learning uses auxiliary estimates to support accurate estimation of causal and structural quantities. One key component is the Riesz representer, which enters Neyman-orthogonal scores and enables square-root-sample-size consistency and asymptotic efficiency. This paper introduces a family of methods for estimating that component by connecting the problem to score matching.

ScoreMatchingRiesz reformulates representer estimation as a score estimation problem. This permits the use of denoising score matching and telescoping density-ratio estimation, which the authors use to stabilize representer estimation. The contribution is a new route to an important auxiliary quantity, linking tools for estimating distributional scores to the requirements of debiased inference.

The paper also introduces the policy path, a parameter describing how policy effects evolve under continuous treatments. The authors show how score matching can estimate this path by smoothly connecting average marginal effects with average policy effects. This provides a more interpretable account of how effects change along a policy path, while using the same score-based perspective that motivates the representer estimators.
icml-2026-scorematchingriesz-score-match.tldr: ScoreMatchingRiesz uses score matching to stabilize Riesz representer estimation and trace policy effects under continuous treatments.

paragraphs: Smoothing typically combines a signal with information from nearby locations. On domains with suitable geometric structure, heat diffusion provides a principled version of this operation through the Laplace operator. Constructing that operator can be difficult when the domain lacks a carefully defined structure, leaving practitioners to use simpler kernels or message-passing layers that introduce boundary bias.

This paper develops smoothing operators from general similarity or adjacency matrices and normalizes them to behave more like diffusion. The construction uses a symmetric version of the Sinkhorn algorithm to rescale positive smoothing operators. It aims to recover desirable structural properties of heat diffusion without requiring the same domain construction used for a geometric Laplacian.

The resulting approach applies to irregular representations including point clouds, sparse voxel grids, and mixtures of Gaussians. The authors show that the normalized operators approximate heat diffusion and retain spectral information from the Laplacian itself. That connection supports applications to shape analysis and matching, extending the usefulness of the construction beyond smoothing signals alone.
icml-2026-sinkhorn-normalization-of-diff.tldr: Symmetric Sinkhorn normalization turns general smoothing operators into diffusion-like operators useful for irregular geometric data.

paragraphs: Highlighting important time points may reveal little about why a time-series model makes a prediction. Meaningful evidence can instead reside in frequencies, trends, or other transformed representations. This paper introduces Cross-domain Integrated Gradients, which moves feature attribution into domains connected to the time domain by an invertible, differentiable transformation.

The derivation extends Integrated Gradients to complex-valued domains, enabling frequency-based explanations while preserving path independence and completeness. The transformation requirement defines which alternative domains the method supports. This lets an explanation address the structure of a signal that matters to the task, rather than only locating influential observations along the original timeline.

The authors validate the method with controlled mechanistic experiments, faithfulness tests, perturbation-stability tests, and real-world cases. Applications examine whether predictions depend on heart-rate frequencies or interference, epileptic sources or artifacts, and trends or seasonal components. These studies reveal behavior missed by time-domain saliency. An accompanying library supports TensorFlow, native PyTorch, and Captum, making the approach available across those modeling tools.
icml-2026-time-series-saliency-maps-expl.tldr: Cross-domain Integrated Gradients explains time-series predictions through frequencies and other valid transformed representations.

paragraphs: The Gilbert–Pollak conjecture concerns how much shorter a Steiner minimum tree can be than a Euclidean minimum spanning tree for the same finite set of planar points. It proposes a lower bound of approximately 0.866 on their length ratio. This paper develops an LLM-based system to improve the certified lower bound, previously reported as 0.824.

The system asks LLMs to generate geometric lemmas that obey specified rules and are implemented as executable code. Those lemmas are assembled into specialized verification functions that yield theoretically certified lower bounds. Reflection drives progressive refinement of the lemmas, connecting language-model proposals to a mathematical verification process.

The authors report a new certified lower bound of 0.8559, obtained with thousands of LLM calls. This advances the bound toward the conjectured value while leaving a gap to 0.866. The result illustrates a concrete role for LLMs in research mathematics: proposing constrained intermediate ingredients that can be refined and incorporated into a system producing certified conclusions.
icml-2026-towards-solving-the-gilbert-po.tldr: An LLM-guided system generates verifiable geometric lemmas and raises the certified Steiner-ratio lower bound to 0.8559.

paragraphs: Removing unwanted concepts or data from a diffusion model can also damage capabilities that should remain. This paper formulates that tension as constrained optimization: keep the updated model close to the pretrained model while explicitly requiring separation from the distributions targeted for unlearning. Preservation becomes the objective, and removal is expressed through constraints.

The authors develop three formulations based on reverse KL divergence, forward KL divergence, and likelihood constraints. The first two generalize existing concept- and data-unlearning approaches, while the likelihood formulation offers a new alternative. Despite the nonconvex KL constraints, they establish strong duality for all three problems, characterize optimal target distributions, and derive primal–dual algorithms.

Experiments show that the KL-constrained method achieves better retention–unlearning trade-offs than weight-based baselines for both concepts and data. The likelihood-based method matches baseline unlearning effectiveness while better preserving retained concepts. These findings connect the mathematical formulation to the practical goal of removing targeted content while limiting disruption to the rest of the model’s behavior.
icml-2026-unlearning-in-diffusion-models.tldr: Constrained optimization gives diffusion-model unlearning explicit removal targets and improves the trade-off between forgetting and retention.

paragraphs: Some prediction errors arise from uncertainty inherent in the data. This paper argues that such aleatoric uncertainty also matters during training: it makes the learning signal stochastic and can obstruct optimization. Tabular deep-learning methods differ substantially in how well they handle that challenge, offering a possible explanation for part of their performance differences.

The authors examine numerical feature embeddings, advanced ensembles, retrieval-augmented models, and tabular Prior-Fitted Networks through this perspective. They find that the benefits of these design choices can be partly attributed to implicit mechanisms that help them perform under high data uncertainty. This provides a shared explanation for improvements that otherwise arise from quite different model designs.

The analysis also produces a practical change: a new, more effective numerical feature embedding method informed by the uncertainty perspective. The contribution therefore connects an explanation of existing methods to an improvement in one of their components. Its central claim is partial attribution: coping with uncertain training signals helps explain modern tabular methods’ success alongside their other benefits.
icml-2026-unveiling-the-role-of-data-unc.tldr: Handling data uncertainty partly explains successful tabular deep-learning designs and motivates a better numerical feature embedding.
